explain.say: See the left side, chimpanzees? They use simple tools, live in groups, and some groups have their own habits, like cracking nuts with stones, which young chimps learn by watching. Humans and chimps share about 98 to 99 percent of the DNA that can be lined up and compared. Does that surprise you?

explain.say: Back to the right side, humans. We have language with grammar, so we can talk about the past, the future and things that are not real. And we pile up culture: each generation adds to what the last one knew, so we went from stone tools to spaceships. Which human skill do you think matters most?

explain.say: Scientists, philosophers and religions answer what makes us human in different ways, from language and culture to conscience and the soul. Most agree that our big shared imagination and cooperation stand out. Brilliant! Challenge: ask three people what they think makes us human, and compare their answers.

faq.q: What makes humans different from other animals?
faq.a: Scientists point to language with grammar, complex tool-making, cooperating in huge groups, and culture that builds up over generations. Philosophers and religions add ideas like conscience and the soul. Many abilities, like tool use and caring, are shared with other animals in simpler forms.
Chimpanzees use tools like sticks and stones, hunt and share meat, comfort each other, and pass on local habits by watching. Jane Goodall first saw them making tools in Tanzania in 1960.

faq.q: What can humans do that chimpanzees cannot?
faq.a: Humans use complex language with grammar, build complex technology, cooperate with millions of strangers, write things down, and build on knowledge from earlier generations.

faq.q: How big is the human brain?
faq.a: An adult human brain weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kilograms, roughly three times the size of a chimpanzee brain. It has a very large cortex, especially the front part used for planning and self-control.
asks: Is the human brain the biggest?

faq.q: How much DNA do humans share with chimpanzees?
faq.a: When the parts of our DNA that line up are compared, humans and chimpanzees differ by only about 1.2 percent. Counting larger pieces that are missing or added, the difference is a bit bigger, about 4 percent.

facts: The Chimpanzee Sequencing Consortium (2005) found about 1.2 percent difference in aligned DNA between humans and chimpanzees.
Humans did not descend from chimpanzees; both share a common ancestor that lived roughly 6 to 7 million years ago.
Jane Goodall first saw wild chimpanzees making and using tools at Gombe, Tanzania, in 1960.
